title: Finite relaxation protocols with minimal dissipation
authors: Ben Ansbacher, Harrison Hartle, Abhishek Yadav, Jan Korbel, David H. Wolpert
abstract: Work extraction from nonequilibrium systems is a major challenge across biological, chemical, physical, and engineering systems. Idealized protocols generally require a quasistatic relaxation stage in which the Hamiltonian is gradually adjusted through a continuum of intermediaries. Here, we consider protocols restricted to a finite number $N$ of intermediary Hamiltonians, consisting of a sequence of quench-relax steps. We determine the sequence of quenches that minimizes the dissipated work, which can be expressed in terms of a recurrence involving the Lambert function. The optimal sequence converges to the Fisher-Rao geodesic, saturating known leading-order dissipation bounds at large $N$. We obtain lower bounds on work extraction from a nonequilibrium distribution as a function of its Fisher-Rao distance to equilibrium. We extend and apply the framework in two simple models: (i) an optical trap experiment, showing that the optimal intermediary distribution can be bimodal even for unimodal initial and final distributions, and (ii) an enzyme-catalyzed reaction, showing that that accounting for relaxation time in addition to dissipation can favor barrier-lowering.
summary: This work develops a theory for minimizing energy dissipation when extracting work from non-equilibrium systems using a finite sequence of controlled quenches. By relating the optimal protocols to the Fisher-Rao geodesic, the authors establish quantitative lower bounds on the maximum extractable work. The framework is successfully applied to model complex physical processes, including optical trapping and enzyme kinetics.
main_problem: The paper determines the optimal sequence of intermediary Hamiltonians for work extraction from non-equilibrium systems when restricted to a finite number of quench-relax steps, aiming to minimize dissipated work.
main_result: The minimal dissipated work scales asymptotically as the square of the Fisher-Rao distance divided by $2 eta N$, and a lower bound on extracted work is derived based on this distance.
method: The problem is formulated as minimizing a sum of Kullback-Leibler divergences over a sequence of quenches, leading to optimal intermediaries defined by a recurrence relation involving the Lambert W function.
model_or_system: The analysis covers general non-equilibrium systems, extending to specific models like optical traps (1D Gaussian distributions) and enzyme-catalyzed reactions (3-state Markov chains).
key_observables: Dissipated work ($W_{	ext{diss}}$), extracted work ($W_{	ext{ext}}$), and the Fisher-Rao distance ($d_{	ext{FR}}$).
important_parameters: The number of steps ($N$), inverse temperature ($ eta$), and the coupling/rate parameters ($\delta, \epsilon$) in the applied models.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is the restriction to a finite number ($N$) of quench-relax steps, and in applications, assumptions about timescales (e.g., separation of timescales in catalysis) are made.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate optimal intermediary distributions (sometimes bimodal) compared to geodesics, show the scaling of mean dissipated work with $N$, and schematically depict the enzyme-catalyzed reaction process.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the general theory of finite relaxation protocols minimizing KL divergence sums, deriving the optimal intermediary form using the Lambert W function, and then applying this framework to concrete examples like optical traps and enzyme catalysis.
why_interesting: It provides rigorous, quantitative bounds on non-equilibrium work extraction, connecting fundamental thermodynamic concepts (dissipation) to geometric measures (Fisher-Rao distance) in a discrete, step-wise manner.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

FIG. 4. Schemtic of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction as modeled in Sec. IV B. Before the enzyme arrives, the substrate is in a meta-stable distribution, ρ0, dominated by the microstate B (bound) representing the substrate before reaction. The enzyme arrives and attaches by van der Waals forces, corre- sponding to an effective quench H0 →H′. In the presence of the enzyme, the system relaxes to the equilibrium associated with H′. The enzyme eventually disconnects due to ther- mal fluctuations, corresponding to a second effective quench, H′ →H0. The system finally relaxes to the equilibrium of the original Hamiltonian, πH0, which is dominated by microstate U (unbound).
